title: Wayseeking Mind
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny tells the story of how Zen practice came into a life that begins in Eugene, Oregon, among runners at Hayward Field and the legend of Steve Prefontaine. Reizan describes the memorial for Pre, where 7,000 people sit through a running clock and applaud an imaginary final half mile. In a hospital room, Reizan's father says "there's a time when you have to let go" and mouths the Lord's Prayer during last rites, and that sight sets the search in motion. Alan Watts tapes and the line "We die and we do not die" in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind follow, then a bicycle trip, Vermont, and a Bodhidharma sticker on the dashboard of Tim's van in Bellingham.

sentences.text: This is a wayseeking mind talk, for anyone who's not familiar with that.
It's a traditional talk about how I came to Zen practice.
In that sense, it's a unique talk for each person.
I've definitely struggled in putting together this talk.
I think most people who do it struggle with it, each for their own reasons.
I came to be a Buddhist when I was 19 years old.
This year I'll be turning 50, so that's a long time.
Coming to Buddhist practice at a young age, there were a lot of things going on in my early life that led me to that.
After working with this talk quite a while, I think I'm probably only going to get up to about that point, which is the interesting part anyway.
After you get to practice, it's all the same old, same old.
Another part about working on this talk that was difficult: I realized I had a lot of grieving about this particular period of my life.
I found myself overriding areas that involved people that have passed away, people important to me.
I'll try to give you a little bit of the future as I'm talking about the past, so you can put a couple of those pieces together.
Anyway, I was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, in 1960.
My family lived there only for one year before moving back to my parents' college town, Eugene, Oregon.

My father was a kind, quick-witted, humorous man who grew up in Detroit, spent his summers at the old family place that my great-great-great-great grandfather built on an island near Canada, and had followed his older brother, my Uncle David, out west.
My mother was the sharp-as-a-tack only daughter of an Eastern Oregon sawmill foreman and his wife, the oldest of four daughters, which formed the matriarchy of my closest family relations.

Almost weekly as I was growing up, during the years I was three and four in Eugene, my older sister would take me on a walk across campus to my father's office, and we always stopped to go through the university's Asian art exhibits at the museum.
Being children who like to repeat experiences, we always went to see the same things.
There were the bronze Buddha heads, the stone-cut relief carvings of Hindu deities, the mystical Taoist priest robes, jade carvings, the spring and autumn scrolls, the Korean dolls.
And there was the fully appointed Chinese Emperor's throne room, where we always ducked the velvet ropes and sat on the thrones.
I had to sit on the smaller one because I was the little brother.
And there was the outdoor courtyard, reflecting, with raindrops splattering the surface, where it was formal and quiet, and I always had to be told it was time to go.
When I was four, my brother was born, and soon after my father had his first heart attack and open heart surgery at age 42.
From then on we were always admonished to be careful, not stress out my dad or make loud noises, and the specter of his illness was always present.
At age five, we moved to Birch Lane in the nicer neighborhood on the wooded ridge overlooking town.
Down the hill was a place I called the Magic Woods.
Strange and good things always happened in the Magic Woods.
And sometimes when I was there, I thought I could understand what the crows overhead were saying.
Up the hill were more woods and Jeffrey Alvarado's house, where at age five we would make campfires and smoke cigarettes, and eventually we burned down the neighbor's woodshed.
I had to do a little sit-down with the city fire marshal, and I couldn't play with Jeffrey Alvarado anymore.
Now, the first time I remember anyone saying "on your mark, get set, go" was the summer I was five.

A few days after moving to Birch Lane, my mother had taken me and my new best friend, Burn, down to the all-comers track meet at the university, and I was running the 75-yard dash for five- and six-year-olds down the middle of the grass infield of Hayward Field, which was across the street from my grade school.

Hayward Field has become the Mecca of American track and field, and Eugene is always on the short list, including places like Helsinki, Berlin, Rome, a few others of the world's premier track and field cities.
All of this started really happening during my growing up, and mostly because of the Oregon coach, Bill Bowerman, who also was the one organizing these all-comer meets.

During those years the premier meet was the Oregon Twilight Invitational, where at the moment of sundown on a spring evening, Bowerman would try to see how many of his athletes he could put under four minutes in the mile.
There were times I saw as many as five go under the barrier in one race.
Coming out of second grade, they said I might have to repeat the grade.
I got diagnosed with a condition that no one else seemed to have in those days, ADD, and the doctors wanted to put me on Ritalin.
It was like the Matrix, you know, take the green pill or the red pill, except this time it was take this pill or repeat second grade, so I took the pill.
But if anyone had asked me, I would have told them there was nothing wrong, and the reason I didn't get my schoolwork done was because school, and especially math, was stupid.
I just couldn't make myself do the assignments, and taking the pill never really changed that.
So I spent my entire school career being 25 or 30 assignments behind every semester in math, and having to make it all up at the end.
What made the whole thing worse was my evil third grade teacher, Ms.

Norwood, who believed that classroom management involved publicly paddling us on the bottom with a selection from her drawer of toy baseball bats, and making everyone's business everyone else's business.
She told all the kids I was on medication for a mental condition.
This resulted in years of teasing.

One thing I realize now that I unconsciously did to compensate was to cultivate a wide assortment of friendships as a counteraction to the cliquishness that the teasing seemed to represent, and I found that my less popular friends teased me much less than my more popular friends.
Now, my father was a quiet and confirmed Christian, and he took us three kids to church, St.
Mary's Episcopal, not with great regularity, but occasionally.
I remember just about nothing about the teachings, but I remember the rhythm: down to the kneeling board to pray, back into the pew, back down to pray.

I didn't know what we were meant exactly to do when praying, because no one ever gave instructions, but there was something about it that always made me wonder, because this was where we spoke to God, right?
And it seemed significant that there were no instructions for this.
I guess I took that as a very open-handed methodology, some acknowledgement of all we couldn't pretend to know.
I remember Palm Sundays.

I remember the day they would give out potted pansies in Sunday school, which I mostly thought was a ploy to keep us children doing something else while the parents were off doing something much more interesting, which they would not tell us about.

I remember many rainy Sundays with my clip-on bow tie and white shirt too tight at the collar because it had been too long since the last time it was worn and I had grown, head feeling light, reading the Sunday comics in the car on the way home, which always made me somewhat nauseous.
Then the too-sugary Easter basket and the syrupy pancakes, and then feeling rather ill.
By 13 I got confirmed, and there was a little youth group thrown in, I'm not sure what for, and then we didn't really go anymore.
My mother never went to church.
Being, as was the whole matriarchy of her side of the family, agnostic or atheistic, I never really knew, because religion was never spoken of in our home or with my relatives.

And I think this is why we stuck quite closely to this branch of the family, because, for instance, Uncle David's wife was reported to be some sort of evangelical brand of faith that my mother could not abide by.
One result of this was a sort of denial of death that went on throughout my life with my family, in that my grandmother and all the great aunties never had funerals when they died.
Another elemental part of my growing up was the beach.
Every summer for almost a month my family would move to the coast and stay in a cabin on the beach with no telephone and no television.
My days were spent shoeless on the beach, and because of the age gap between myself and my older sister and younger brother, mostly alone.
I mostly spent my time setting up the task for myself of building elaborate beach forts.
When not building forts, I would scour the beach in search of the item that hovered in my imagination as the most prized of all beachcombing finds, the Japanese glass fishing float.
My sense of geography was a very direct and palpable thing for me growing up.
Japan was somewhere right over there, over the ocean horizon and not so far, as evidenced by the fact that, although I never found one, those glass orbs did sometimes come up on these beaches.
Most places seemed far away.
Oregon, especially back when I was growing up, was an extremely provincial place.
No place was thought to be better.
Why vacation anywhere else when you can live here?
And those Californians in their slow Winnebagos creeping along the ocean cliffs.
Well, we should just build a wall at the border.
I never traveled anywhere much out of the state until I was almost 20, and never flew in a plane, except once briefly to Seattle for 20 minutes, until I was 24.
We had a neighborhood kids' newspaper run by our stay-at-home but overeducated moms, the Grasshopper, that ran 10 issues each spring for 10 years.
The Grasshopper picnic each year was the event of the season.
The older kids usually got to collectively write a feature or interview each issue, and one day my mother brought into the Grasshopper clubhouse Steve Prefontaine.
Prefontaine was the now legendary Oregon runner who at one time held all six American records from 2,000 to 10,000 meters.

This day at the Grasshopper he was the precocious and fiery 19-year-old freshman phenomenon from Coos Bay who had broken the prep national two-mile record and very nearly taken the NCAA cross country crown that fall, battling Jerry Lindgren down to the final step.
We each got autographs, a torn-off page of yellow steno pad.
I still have mine, a prized possession, a full Steve Prefontaine.

It being soon after that the simple moniker would be all he would have time to jot on the meet programs, T-shirts and arms of the hordes of kids who flocked to him at every meet, because even then the stands of Hayward Field had begun to boil with the thunderous signature stamping, a rhythmic confluence of athlete and spectator beyond what anyone had heard before, that echoed: "Go Pre, go Pre, go Pre."
Now even to this day in Eugene the story goes, and I witnessed it many times myself so I say it's true, that at a meet the clouds would always part when Pre stepped on the Hayward Field track.
As I got a little older, my running abilities began to show themselves.
In junior high I was winning races, setting school records.
You can't know too much about me until you know a little bit about Roosevelt Junior High School, Roosevelt Rough Riders.
Four years before I got to Roosevelt there had been a student revolution, a sit-down strike, grievances and a new curriculum which involved no requirements and no grades.
The annual musical theater production the year before I entered school was a full-scale stage production of the rock opera Tommy since 1971.
At any time of the school day you could walk out the back into the large field and wade through the tall grass and find six or twelve students in a circle smoking pot.
One time, I can't remember what class this was for, a self-made assignment, I spent an entire day inside of a cardboard box.

I think the idea was something about sensory deprivation, and I was a little dismayed at the light leaking around the edges, even though I was inside of a storage closet, and at the fact that by listening to the patterns of feet outside the door I could tell which period of class it was.
But there were moments in the dark when I lost complete track of time, and I was amazed when the door opened and somebody told me the school day was over, because I thought it was too soon.
Pre was acting as a mentor at the junior high, and we'd see him running, usually up and down the halls from one thing to another.

As things progressed we shared a track with the high school, and as we were getting a little bit older still, at the junior high we were allowed in our offseason to start training with the high school.

The story goes, one day I went over with a couple other boys, and I said to the coach, Harry Johnson, who we'd never met before, it had been pre-arranged that we were going to come over, but I said, "Hi, Coach Johnson, we're the boys from Roosevelt," and he said, "We only have men on this team," which was really the perfect thing to say and won us over completely, because our school theater production, now for two years running at Roosevelt, had been a modernized adaptation of Taming of the Shrew entitled Miz, and calling any 14-year-old female at my school "girl" got you an immediate lecture.
But nobody ever called us men.
That was the situation we were working with, Harry.
The South Eugene high school track program in the 70s was the best high school track program, and our work was pretty well laid out for us: twice-a-day workouts every day.
In high school I had a class first period that was called running, which was just a way for me to have time to do my morning workout.
Through the years in high school, starting ninth grade, South began setting national high school records in relay events, and I was able to be part of one of those in my junior year.
There were individual national high school records by various friends of mine and an amazing long string of state championships that went for over 12 years.
We never lacked in self-confidence, and it was a time when a kid could dream that maybe he too could be an Olympian.
But at the end of my ninth grade year came the day that Pre died in a car accident just in front of the Alvarado's house.
A few days later, 7,000 of us filled the old wooden East grandstands, where just the night before Pre died we had been watching his final race.
In the final mile he had moved away from everyone; no one could stay with him.
Frank Shorter was in the race and afterwards said he was just beyond me at that point.

He missed his own American record by less than two seconds, and you'll know that it's that race if you see a picture of him wearing a black singlet, because it's the only race in his life that he wore a black singlet.
We filed into these grandstands, and the stadium clock was started and set to stop at what some felt would have been for Pre a satisfactory world record for three miles.
As the clock ran, first Bowerman, and then Shorter, and finally Kenny Moore, who besides having gotten fourth in the Munich Marathon was also a world-class sportswriter, spoke.
He said he conceived of the sport as service, in the way an artist serves.
Without that he would never have given us all the records, they were out beyond winning or losing, which a runner does for himself.
They came from those furious minutes near the end of a race when his relentlessness and our excitement blended into a joyous thunder.
All of us who now say "I had no idea how much this man meant to me" do so because we didn't realize how much we meant to him.
He was our glory and we his.
Then he stepped away from the podium, then stepped back and said, "There are two minutes on the clock.
He could run a half a mile."
Then we all waited in silence, 7,000 people, for a minute and a half.

Nothing had been indicated of how this would finish other than the clock running out, but with 30 seconds to go, I, like everyone else looked over at the 200 meters to go mark, and as the imaginary runner was coming around the bend, a truly amazing display of public ceremony spontaneously unfolded.
First from the left and then traveling all down the grandstand, the crowd applauded in a rolling wave that finally trickled out at the finish line.
It was over, the clock stopped, and the silence swept back to fill the space.
Now the rock outcropping, a couple blocks distance from the house I grew up in, where Pre's MG overturned, has become a devotional site.
At any time, and especially when a major meet is in town, the rock is festooned with offerings: meet ribbons, someone's race numbers from Boston, state championship medals, shoes, t-shirts.
Runners and athletes from all over the world leave items of significance at this spot to remember this person who inspired so many.
That summer my family bought a beach cabin on the coast that we vacationed at, and instead of renting we'd have a place of our own.
My father hired a carpenter, and I came to work too, for 75 cents an hour.
The carpenter was John Pound, a 40-something hippie artist from California whose work vehicle was a VW van with an American flag draped along the whole ceiling inside.
Think Jimmy Buffett plus 40 pounds, and overalls, with a pipe clenched in the corner of his mouth and a wry little Santa Claus twinkle in his eye.
John was a self-taught remodeler, experienced in a lot of things, willing to try something.
He was also an astute observer of the human condition, born from his years in therapy, a very Californian attribute, which I thought was interesting.
He was extremely accepting and fond of me, and was the only person in my life who's ever been able to call me Bobby, with any sense of acceptance from me.
Living alone on the coast had its difficulties in loneliness.
At 15 years old, living alone with a bicycle to get around, I had no telephone or TV, only the radio at night to keep me company.
The wide-stretched Oregon beaches are not the sort of place to go and meet people; it's the kind of place people go to be alone.
But I enjoyed it well enough, and I came back the following summer and did the same thing.
In high school my friend Jeff, another runner, and I had started getting into bowhunting.
I'd always done archery since childhood, taught by my mother, who had been taught by my grandfather.
I'd always been inspired by my grandfather, who had died when I was 11, a man with a quiet and deeply assured bearing.

He was a hunter and fisherman who attended his half-acre garden at his place on the banks of the Rogue River, where he pulled steelhead out from his walking dock, and where he would wash newly pulled carrots for me in the irrigation ditch beside the grape arbors and raspberries.

Now on weekend trips Jeff and I would drive high into the dark coast range on early foggy mornings before dawn and stalk through the woods, in camouflage clothing covered in deer musk scent, moving as quietly as possible and listening.

At other times we'd travel over the mountains to camp in the junipers and stalk through the hard frost sagebrush hunting jackrabbits, which with a bow, it's no wonder we never got one, but we did get shots.

We never managed to take a shot at a deer, though I did have one encounter in the deeply twilight woods: a silhouette that looked like it had antlers, my hand trembling on the string, the darkness growing, and inside the jackhammer heart pounding, my legs quivering, sweat immediately beading up, almost feeling like I couldn't breathe.

After this I decided I probably did not want to go through with the whole killing thing, and when I went to college I became a vegetarian, which for me was really an extension of the same thoughts about food.
Each year in high school I would ride my bike on one spring weekend out to Mount Pisgah on the edge of town and camp out alone for the night.
On these trips I would always try to go back into the woods to find deer.
I'd try to get as close as possible and feel the deer's presence and become part of its world.
I felt I had an almost mystical feeling about them, and when I could have an encounter like that, it always felt special.

Now, the summer before my senior year, a few blocks away, my dad's best friend from college, Ed Frazier, an editorial page columnist for the Eugene Register-Guard, got up after dinner, went into the bathroom, took out a pistol and shot himself in the head.
He didn't leave a note.
I can only imagine what my father's feelings were.

It wasn't as though we had the kind of relationship where he would come lean on me, but one day a couple weeks after it happened he turned to me with this pained look and simply said, "Why would someone do that?" and I knew what he was referring to.
Then at some point that fall he had another heart attack.
He was in the hospital for a while, then some rest, then back to work in a limited way.
It was scary, but I guess filtering through the denial, I believed he was going to get through this already.
Then on New Year's Eve day, coming back from a snow camping trip, Jeff and I spontaneously decided to stop and try and climb a huge cliff we saw.
We only got so far, and then I kicked loose a 300-pound boulder, and the boulder and I went careening down the slope together.
It rolled over my leg twice, then was coming for my head.
I got my hands on it and finally pushed myself clear.
My right calf was crushed, but the bone wasn't broken.
I was six weeks on crutches, each day to the pool to swim and keep fitness, then two weeks walking, two weeks jogging, finally actual running.
Then while helping with field events I got hit in the leg, in the same spot, by a discus.
Finally I made it to the district meet, but by that point my father, back at home, was growing sicker and sicker.
At the district meet only the top two qualified for state.
By the top of the final turn I'd forged up to the shoulder of the early leader, but then two more came up, and for a moment we were four abreast, and then that was it.
There was nothing left.
The three drifted away.
I was a second behind the line, but at this point it didn't really matter; I felt at least I was running.
Someone was waving to me beside the track.
It was my father in his wheelchair.
He had insisted that my sister bring him to the meet.
I had no idea he would be there, but he waved me over and we hugged, and it really made the whole experience much more tolerable for that moment.
But not long after that the call came down the stairs in the middle of the night, and the family flew into action like some kind of drill team.
I was given the keys, and driving maybe 90 miles an hour, made it to the hospital in just about three minutes.
Caught up with adrenaline, I simply followed my father on the gurney back into the back room while the rest of the family collapsed in the waiting room.
In the back room they had him on a machine that went beep, beep.
He was talking with me softly for a bit, then he closed his eyes for a minute, then the beep, beep sound stopped.
I touched his shoulder and he opened his eyes again, and the beeping started back, and he said, "What?" and I said, "Nothing, it's okay."
He was in intensive care for a couple days, and then one moment they wheeled him out into a regular room.
I knew this meant that they decided there was nothing more to do.
I found a minute and slipped into the room so I could see him alone.
He told me there was not much else to do at this point.
Feeling desperate, feeling like there had to be something I could say that would change the situation, I said, "Dad, I've seen a lot of guys give up.
Isn't there something more you can do?"
And he said, "Bob, there's a time when you have to let go."
A day or so later the priest was called in for the last rites.
We were basically living on the couches in the waiting area down the hall.
I hadn't been home or barely eaten anything for days.
I stood at the foot of the bed as the priest gave the last rites.
My father was on his side, and when the priest began the Lord's Prayer, my father's hands moved in front of his face in prayer position, and I could see his lips mouthing the words in unison.
Right there I made a decision, born from seeing the clear faith that my father had.
I decided that I would seek out, as far as I could, what life and death was for me in my life, and that I would start now.
I had to finish up my senior year of high school, and we had the state meet.
I hadn't qualified, but the mile relay was an option.
There was one other boy; the coach put us through a time trial, and we ran exactly the same time.
My coach said, "I'm going to choose the other boy, because I don't want you to potentially lose right now.
It's not going to be good for you, with everything that you've lost so far."
It came down to the last event.
Us and another team were even in the score: if we won the mile relay we'd win the meet, if they won the mile relay they'd win the meet.
I watched, and they won.
We lost the state meet.
It was the only time in 13 years straight that to my high school had lost the state meet, but it didn't really matter.
I couldn't really feel what that would mean.

It took me a long time to really be thankful that he had not put me in that race, because although for years I thought I could have beaten that guy, I realize now it would have been just as likely that it wouldn't have happened that way, and if it hadn't, then I would have to live with that.
There was no work available, things were getting sort of economically depressed, but I went to the coast anyway to find John.
I told him about my father, and he was like the only person in my life who was able to really take me aside, really talk to me like a peer.
We talked late into the night.
He took me out on the beach.
He told me all about my father, because he'd worked with him closely on remodeling our cabin.

It was really important, and even though I never really worked with John again, later on I would continue to come back to visit him whenever I had the chance, just because he was a person in my life who had that role, and he really helped me.
He told me about his own father's death, how he had come in and been the one to find him.
He called it "Dad's last scene": the bedspread pulled aside, the angina pills thrown across the floor.
I felt like he was somebody who could relate.
I started out running for Oregon that fall, and I was in the architecture school.
I was living with guys, also on the team, who were from my high school; we were rooming together.

The roommate situation didn't work out and we had to break it up in the middle of the year, and I went searching and found a household of people, mostly who weren't students, living far away from campus, and I moved in with them.
They were all older than me, and one of my roommates was a guy named Steve, this sort of reclusive pothead who just stayed in his room all the time.
He went away for two weeks for Christmas, and when he came back, when he walked in the door, it was the most radical transformation I've ever seen in a person.
Before, Steve was clean-shaven, bright-eyed, well dressed, and had had a religious conversion.

He had become born again on the airplane headed out to Tennessee; he had seen all the people as souls, and he had thrown away his drugs and had had what seemed to be a very genuine, heartfelt conversion.
One day I was standing in the doorway of his room talking, and I glanced at his Bible, and he said, "Are you interested in taking a look at that?"
I said, "Yeah."
He said, "Actually, why don't you just have it?
I'll give it to you."
He gave me his Bible, and I thought, that's a sign; I'm going to read this from start to back.
Shortly after that I was in a lecture at the university, a wide-ranging, rambling course, and there was a Chinese [unclear: "structures"] professor up there throwing slides up.
He threw one up of [unclear: "a die"] a bunch of crazy diagrams, and he said, "Oh, and this is from the I Ching, pattern of the universe," and he switched to the next slide.
I went, "What is that?"
And that very night I was walking home at about 10 o'clock, and I stopped by a bookstore and was just perusing books in the philosophy section, as I used to do, and there was this book, the I Ching.
I thought, I'm going to buy that.

So here I was reading the Bible and the I Ching, and after a while I started realizing that the Bible was really kind of a mishmash, but when I would get to those points where Jesus spoke, I thought, hey, this guy's got something going on.
I started developing a really [unclear: "soft in touch"] sort of feeling about Jesus, and wondering to myself, I wonder if this is something I should take farther.
One day I was walking home again and I met a very young boy, maybe a year younger than me or so, somewhat disheveled, standing on the street corner preaching the Lord's word.
I engaged him in conversation, feeling like I wanted to be open to people, and he said, "Let's go back to my apartment and testify to God."
I said okay, and we went back to his little hovel of a place, and we got down on the floor amidst his junk and dirty laundry, with our hands on the Bible.
He said, "Do you take Jesus into your heart?" and I said, feeling like, okay, this is the moment, if I can't do it here, where could I do it: "It's just not there.
I'm sorry."
And I left.
Sometime during that school year I overheard just this one piece of a conversation as I was standing in the architecture school.
Somebody said, "Have you ever heard Alan Watts speak?
He has a very mesmerizing voice."
Months later, with my friend Matt, also a runner from high school, hanging out, no job, summertime, bored, Matt said, "What should we do?"
I said, "You know what, let's go to the university listening library.
I heard this guy Alan Watts, and he has a really mesmerizing voice."
So, not knowing anything else, up for an adventure, we went to the listening library.
It's really significant that I had actually earlier in the year taken Indian art and Chinese art.
I just spontaneously signed up for these courses, and of course, dutifully, at some point they want to tell you something about the religion that you're looking at.
all the art of, and there was a very quick rendition of the four noble truths.
My first impression of that, when I jotted it down in my class notes, was: no way.
So here we are in the listening library, and they have the little cassette tape recorder where you plug in the earphones.
We get two sets of earphones and sit at the table looking across at each other.
They had a set of tapes, *The Essential Alan Watts*.
I figured that must be pretty good.
There were about ten lectures, so we'd listen to two each day, five days for the whole week.

We came back every day for five days and listened to ten hours of Alan Watts lectures, just looking at each other with these little glimmers of recognition flashing in our eyes as we were listening to all of this, going like, yeah.
Right outside the listening library door was a stack of books, and all of the Asian religion books were right there.
So that summer I read *Three Pillars of Zen*, I read *Zen Keys*, I read *Selling Water by the River*, I read a whole slew of Zen books.
And of course I read *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*, which is the book that impressed me the most.
Even if you're asking today, there's really only one line I remember from the book.

After the prologue, the fun simile about beginner's mind and expert mind, the book starts proper, and after an introductory paragraph, at the beginning of the second paragraph of the first chapter, he says:
*After some years we will die.
If we think that it is the end of our life, this will be the wrong understanding.
But on the other hand, if we think that we do not die, this is also wrong.
We die and we do not die.
That is the right understanding.*
I thought to myself, well, I've never heard anything so clear in my whole life.
So I went home and I started to try to meditate.

I got some cushions, I sat down in my bedroom, I crossed my legs, I got myself plumb and straight and whatever else I thought I should have been doing, and within about thirty seconds I started getting this feeling.
Then I thought, I must be becoming enlightened, and I was doing it all wrong and hyperventilating.
I passed out and hit the floor.
Well, by the end of that summer Matt and I were headed back to school, but we were done with it.
We decided, okay, one more year and then we get to drop out.
I wasn't running on the team anymore, my architecture class was conflicted, and I had a problem relating to the coach, because he had a problem relating to a lot of people.
I was training on my own.
I was now living with another high school running friend, also an architecture student, Jim, and basically trying to keep myself fit and wondering what the next thing in life was.
How are we doing on time?
I'm not sure when we're supposed to stop.
The watch says quarter to four.
Well, it only gets better.
I'll give you the quick wrap-up.
I only have about thirty years to cover, but I swear I can do this really fast.
Matt and I did go on a bicycle trip, six weeks, 1500 miles, and true to form we barely left the state of Oregon.
Well, two days in California.
Then I transferred to the University of Arizona and lived in Tucson for four years.
I ran on the track team.
I completed what for me was really a personal goal, to run NCAA track.
Not that I was that good, not that I ever got to compete that much, but just that I got to be there.
I was running with South Eugene people; there were three other South Eugene runners on the team, people I knew, close friends.
I changed majors.
I was studying general fine arts, which was music, which I had done my whole life, creative writing, which I had never done, and photography, which I had never done.
I simply said, oh, I'm going to go be a photographer, I'm going to go be a poet, even though I'd never written anything.
In architecture school for two years I had never had time to even take my freshman English class, so I was starting my third year of college without having taken Composition 101.
But I was also pretty sure that I didn't know what I wanted to do, or I didn't really want college to be some sort of indicator of what you can do with your life, that type of thing.
So I didn't have any plans.
When I got done with the running career and got done with college, there was a girlfriend at the end of college who was studying Kundalini yoga at the 3HO ashram on campus.
I was pretty much a strong yoga student for about a year there and got really involved with that community.
Then I went to my fallback, which was the bicycle.
I put whatever little things I owned into storage, I put what I needed on the bicycle, and I resolutely decided to decide not to decide where I was going.
I told everyone I knew that I was not going to call.
I told my mother I was not going to call her, and I took off.
Ten days later I was facing this ocean of sagebrush, the east side of the Navajo reservation.
I wasn't sure I could even get across.
The maps were sketchy.
I was riding through the heat, through canyons, and finally I came to the base of some mountains called the Jemez Mountains.
This was in the age before the internet.

Trying to find out about things, I had gone to the university library before, to find out names of different spiritual communities and places, and I had this name, Jemez Bodhi Mandala, but no address.
I figured maybe it's around here.
So I stopped into a little two-pump gas station, bought a Snickers bar, and said, is there a Buddhist monastery around here?
And I think the answer was yes, ten miles up the road.
So I went up there, and they were hosting a massage retreat for a month, massage practitioners, and that's where I met who's now my ex-wife.
She was there from Vermont, living in Vermont.
There was a monk there.
He saw me in the office as I was checking out, because I'd been digging ditches for a few days to save money, to pay my way there, and he said, so you're on the road again, huh?
Oh yeah, I gotta go.
He said, well, you'll do okay, you did okay here.
Everybody thought I was her long-lost boyfriend because we had gotten together so quickly.
I ended up bicycling through Colorado, making it to Boulder, but I got really sick.
I had had intestinal flu when I was a kid and was in the hospital for a week at one point, and then it happened again.
I had no money, and I knew I was getting to be in a bad way.
I went to Naropa Institute.
I thought, maybe I'm not going to pull out the Buddhist card, but I'll just say I need some help.
But they said they really didn't have a place to put me up.
I found somebody on the street who said there's a priest that will give you food, so I went to a church and he made me two peanut butter sandwiches and two plums.
That was the last thing I ate for a while.
Then, knowing that I needed to do something, I went up Boulder Canyon, set up my tent and got inside, and I got really, really sick.
Three days later I was sort of staggering out of the tent, and there was a guy on the road, a hitchhiker, and he said, hey friend.
It was this guy Donald Brant, who had been on the road for twelve years.
Vietnam vet, PSA, you know, PTSD, total classic case, antisocial, but he liked relating to people just one-on-one.
He had run some sort of scam on food stamps, and he had seventy-five dollars of food stamps.
He had gone to the store and bought the only thing that he thought was worth anything, which was top ramen.
He had seventy-five dollars' worth of top ramen in his backpack, which coincidentally was just about the only thing I could eat: some soft noodles, a little miso, that was good.
He nursed me back to health for about a week, and then I went down and started working temporary labor, and so I bought him a new tarp.
Pretty much we lived together for three and a half weeks up Boulder Canyon until the cops kicked us out.
I eventually hitchhiked and got to Vermont.
I lived in Vermont for four years and got married there.
My ex-wife was studying with a Native American Tibetan teacher named Dhyani Ywahoo, a woman, and her spiritual center was there.
At one point we lived at Sunray, the spiritual center for her practice, and we wanted her to marry us, but there just seemed to be a communication breakdown.
We ended up having Gopal, her yoga instructor, who was a devotee of Swami Shyam and Swami Sivananda, marry us, outdoors.
We ran at a funky geodesic dome on eighty acres up in the mountains for 230 dollars a month.
I was doing carpentry.
Then we went on the Audubon Expedition Institute, a graduate program.
For two years we traveled around North America on a converted school bus in a consensus educational community and got master's degrees in environmental education, camping out every night.
They had A-frame three-person tents, and I would always select the middle position, which of course nobody wanted, so it was an easy sell.
But it was the only full setting headroom height in the tent.
I would set my watch a half hour early before wake-up and sit zazen between my two tent mates every day.
We hardly ever camped in the same place twice.

We went to the northern tip of Newfoundland and the southern tip of Florida, we came to Washington State, we were in the Southwest, and then I moved to Bellingham, which was really a dark throw at the map.
Near the end of grad school I had been reading *The Mind of Clover*.
When I got to the end of it, I turned it over and started reading again, and I did that about three or four times with that book.
I thought, I want to find out about this practice tradition.
So I called Hawaii, I called Koko An, and I said, is there anybody in the Pacific Northwest who's studying with you?
They said yeah, and they gave me the name of some people in Seattle, and we went and visited them.
They gave us the name of a couple other people who lived in Bellingham, Jack Duffy and Ian Keira.
So we went up and visited them and we said, oh, this is, we're going to move to this town.
They were the only people we knew, and they were actually just about to do a huge remodel on their house, so I instantly had a job building their house.
I practiced with Three Treasures Sangha in Seattle for five years.
During our vacation breaks on the Audubon school, we had times when we were off the school, but we had to be places, we had to just take care of ourselves.
One of those was in San Francisco for a couple of weeks.

We stayed at City Center for about five days, then we backpacked down from Mount Tam to Green Gulch, like I was telling you about the other day, and we stayed at Green Gulch as guest students for five days, which was perfect because we could do our schoolwork and then do this other thing.
I had met Norman then.
On our final evening, at dinner, I met this guy with long hair and a big red beard.
His name was Tim.
We had a really good conversation, and it was one of those small-world things.
I figured, we're heading this way in life, he's going there, I'll never see this person again.
Why would I even think about whether I was going to see him or not?
It was just a nice meeting.
A year and a half or two later I was up in Bellingham, living here now, working as an environmental educator, and I needed to hire somebody to help me with day camp.
I hired this guy Tim, and we worked together for a couple of weeks.
At one point Tim had a VW van, and I got into his van, he was driving me someplace, and there was a sticker, an ink caricature of Bodhidharma, on the dashboard.
On the glove box, yeah, great.
I said, oh, Bodhidharma, and Tim says, Bodhidharma, [unclear: "Dayosha of Zen code"], and I go, before.

It was interesting because on the Audubon school we were required to have our hair above our ears and be clean-shaven, because we were going around to a lot of places and we looked weird enough, and they wanted us to be acceptable.
You know how Tim looked.
Then when we met up again in Bellingham it was all different.
I had a short beard and long hair, and Tim was somewhat similar, and we just looked totally different.
Shortly after that Tim made little flyers that said something like "Zen sitting."
He lived on Harris Street with a little glass front porch, a little space where you'd have maybe three zafus, and that was the beginning of the Bellingham Zen practice group.
I would come when I could.
Probably half the time I would call Tim and tell him I'm calling to tell you I'm not coming, because I was living out of town, I was practicing with another group, I had a baby on the way.
But eventually things just gravitated over.
The interesting thing was that Three Treasures went through this period of time of hunting for a teacher, and I was on this committee to hunt for a teacher.
So I had this whole correspondence with Norman by letter before we ever had any sort of other type of relationship.
In fact Norman was a house guest of mine, because Tim lived in my cabin, which was after.
But Tim and Janet were getting married, and so Norman was the first cabin resident, I guess, when Tim came to get married, our house guest.
I do remember Norman coming in the morning for breakfast and saying hello to our dog, and getting right down and being with the dog, really being with Rose, our dog.
I was very impressed by that.
So anyway, the rest is kind of maybe more that, you know, I've left out a lot of the bad parts.
They're in there, but I suppose it's time to go.
Thank you very much for letting me run on and on and on.
I knew that I would not be able to do it in the allotted time.
Yeah, it doesn't matter, it can't tell time.
Yeah, you gave me the watch.
I don't know, there's one there too, obviously.
But yeah, and Norman said it would all work out somehow, and it did.
Well, thank you very much.

verbatim.text: This is a way seeking mind talk for anyone who's not familiar with that. It's a traditional talk about how I came to Zen practice. In that sense, it's sort of a unique talk for each person. I think I've definitely struggled in putting together this talk. I think most people who do it do struggle with it, each for their own reasons. I came to become a Buddhist when I was 19 years old. This year I'll be turning 50, so that's a long time. Coming to Buddhist practice at a young age, there were a lot of things going on in my early life that led me to that. After working with this talk quite a while, I think I'm probably only going to get up to about that point, which is sort of the

interesting part anyway. After you get to practice, it's all sort of the same old, same old. Another part about working on this talk that was difficult is I realized I had a lot of grieving about this particular period of my life. I found myself overriding areas that involved people that have passed away, people important to me. I'll try and mention I'll try and give you a little bit of the future as I'm talking about the past, so you can kind of put a couple of those pieces together. Anyway, I was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, 1960. My family lived there only for one year before moving to my parents' college town back to Eugene, Oregon. My father was a kind, quick-witted, humorous

man who grew up in Detroit, spent his summers at the old family place that my great-great-great-great grandfather built on an island near Canada and had followed his older brother, my Uncle David, out west. My mother was a sharp-as-tack only daughter of an Eastern Oregon sawmill foreman and his wife, the oldest of four daughters, which formed the matriarchy of my closest family relations. Almost weekly as I was growing up, during the years I was three and four in Eugene, my older sister would take me on a walk across campus to my father's office and we always stopped to go through the university's Asian art exhibits at the museum. And being children who like to repeat experiences, we always went to see the same

things. There were the bronze Buddha heads, the stone-cut relief carvings of Hindu deities, the mystical Taoist priest robes, jade carvings, the spring and autumn scrolls, the Korean dolls. And there was the fully appointed Chinese Emperor's throne room, where we always ducked the velvet ropes and sat on the thrones. I had to sit on the smaller one because I was the little brother. And there was the outdoor courtyard reflecting with raindrops splattering the surface where it was formal and quiet and I always had to be told it was time to go. When I was four, my brother was born and soon after my father had his first heart attack and open heart surgery at age 42. From then on, we were

always admonished to be careful, not stress out my dad or make loud noises and the specter of his illness was always present. At age five, we moved to Birch Lane in the nicer neighborhood on the wooded ridge overlooking town. Down the hill was a place I called the Magic Woods. Strange and good things always happened in the Magic Woods. And sometimes when I was there, I thought I could understand what the crows overhead were saying. Up the hill were more woods and Jeffrey Alvarado's house, where at age five we would make campfires and smoke cigarettes and eventually we burned down the neighbor's woodshed. I had to do a little sit down with the city fire marshal and I couldn't play with

Jeffrey Alvarado anymore. Now the first time I remember anyone saying, on your mark, get set, go. It was the summer I was five. A few days after moving to Birch Lane, my mother had taken me and my new best friend, Burn, down to the all comers track meet at the university and I was running the 75 yard dash for five and six year olds down the middle of the grass infield of Hayward Field, which was across the street from my grade school. Hayward Field has become the Mecca of American track and field and Eugene is always on the short list, including places like Helsinki, Berlin, Rome, a few others of the world's premier track and field cities. All of this started really happening during my

growing up and mostly because of the Oregon coach, Bill Bowerman, who also was the one organizing these all-comer meets. During those years, the premier meet was the Oregon Twilight Invitational, where at the moment of sundown on a spring evening, Bowerman would try to see how many of his athletes he could put under four minutes in the mile. There were times I saw as many as five go under the barrier in one race. Coming out of second grade, they said I might have to repeat the grade. I got diagnosed with a condition that no one else seemed to have in those days, ADD, and the doctors wanted to put me on Ritalin. It was sort of like the matrix, you know, take the green pill and red pill, except this time it was take this pill or

repeat second grade, so I took the pill. But if anyone had asked me, I would have told them there was nothing wrong, and the reason I didn't get my schoolwork done was because school, and especially math, was stupid. I just couldn't make myself do the assignments, and taking the pill never really changed that, so I spent my entire school career being 25 or 30 assignments behind every semester in math, and having to make it all up at the end. What made the whole thing worse was my evil third grade teacher, Ms. Norwood, who believed that classroom management involved publicly paddling us on the bottom with a selection from her drawer of toy baseball bats and making everyone's business everyone else's business, and she told all

the kids I was on medication for a mental condition. This resulted in years of teasing. One thing I realize now that I unconsciously did to compensate was to cultivate a wide assortment of friendships as a counteraction to the clickishness that the teasing seemed to represent, and I found that my less popular friends teased me much less than my more popular friends. Now my father was a quiet and confirmed Christian, and he took us three kids to church, St. Mary's Episcopal, not with great regularity, but occasionally. I remember just about nothing about the teachings, but I remember the rhythm down to the kneeling board to pray, back into the pew, back down to pray. I didn't know what we were meant exactly to do when

praying because no one ever gave instructions, but there was something about it that always made me wonder because this was where we spoke to God, right? And it seemed significant that there were no instructions for this. I guess I took that as a very open-handed methodology, some sort of acknowledgement of all we couldn't pretend to know. I remember Palm Sundays. I remember the day they would give out potted pansies and Sunday school, which I mostly thought was a ploy to keep us children doing something else while the parents were off doing something much more interesting, which they would not tell us about. I remember many rainy Sundays with my clip-on bow tie and white shirt too tight at the collar because it had been too

long since last time it was worn and I had grown, head feeling light, reading the Sunday comics in the car on the way home, which always made me somewhat nauseous. Then the two sugary Easter basket and the syrupy pancakes and then feeling rather ill. By 13 I got confirmed and there was a little youth group thrown in, I'm not sure what for, and then we didn't really go anymore. My mother never went to church. Being as was the whole matriarchy of her side of the family, agnostic or atheistic, I never really knew because religion was never spoken of in our home or with my relatives. And I think this is why we stuck quite closely to this branch of the family because, for instance, Uncle David's wife

was reported to be some sort of evangelical brand of faith that my mother could not abide by. And one result of this was a sort of denial of death that went on throughout my life with my family in that my grandmother and all the great aunties never had funerals when they died. Another elemental part of my growing up was the beach. Every summer for almost a month my family would move to the coast and stay in a cabin on the beach with no telephone and no television. My days were spent shoeless on the beach, and because of the age gap between myself and my older sister and younger brother, mostly alone, I mostly spent my time setting up the task for myself of building elaborate beach forts. When not building forts, I would scour the

beach in search of the item that hovered in my imagination as the most prized of all beach combing finds, the Japanese glass fishing float. My sense of geography was a very direct and palpable thing for me growing up. Japan was somewhere right over there, over the ocean horizon and not so far, as evidenced by the fact that, although I never found one, those glass orbs did sometimes come up on these beaches. Most places seemed far away. Oregon, especially back when I was growing up, was an extremely provincial place. No place was thought to be better. Why vacation anywhere else when you can live here? And those Californians in their slow Winnebago's creeping along the ocean cliffs. Well, we should just build a wall

at the border. I never traveled anywhere much out of the state until I was almost 20 and never flew in a plane except once briefly to Seattle for 20 minutes until I was 24. We had a neighborhood kids newspaper run by our stay at home but overeducated moms, the grasshopper that ran 10 issues each spring for 10 years. The grasshopper picnic each year was the event of the season. The older kids usually got to collectively write a feature or interview each issue and one day my mother brought into the grasshopper clubhouse Steve Prefontaine. Prefontaine was the now legendary Oregon runner who at one time held all six American records from 2,000 to 10,000 meters. This day at the grasshopper he was the precocious and fiery 19-year-old freshman

phenomenon from Coos Bay who had broken the prep national two-mile record and very nearly taken the NCAA cross country crown that fall, battling Jerry Lindgren down to the final step. We each got autographs, a torn off page of yellow Stenol pad, I still have mine, a prized possession, a full of Steve Prefontaine. It soon being after that the simple moniker would be all he would have time to jot on the meat programs, t-shirts and arms of the hordes of kids who flocked to him at every meet because even then the stands of Hayward Field had begun to boil with the thunderous signature stamping a rhythmic confluence of athlete and spectator beyond what anyone had heard before that echoed, go pre, go pre, go pre.

Now even to this day in Eugene the story goes and I witnessed it many times myself so I say it's true that at a meet the clouds would always part when pre stepped on the Hayward Field track. As I got a little older my running abilities began to show themselves. In junior high I was winning races, setting school records. You can't know too much about me until you know a little bit about Roosevelt Junior High School, Roosevelt Rough Riders. Four years before I got to Roosevelt there had been a student revolution, sit down strike grievances and new curriculum which involved no requirements and no grades. The annual musical theater production the year before I entered school was a full-scale

stage production of the rock opera Tommy since 1971. At any time of the school day you could walk out the back into the large field and wade through the tall grass and find six or twelve students in a circle smoking pot. One time, I can't remember what class this was for, a self-made assignment I spent an entire day inside of a cardboard box. I think the idea was something about sensory deprivation and I was a little dismayed at the light leaking around the edges even though I was inside of a storage closet and the fact that by listening to the patterns of feet outside the door I could tell which period of class it was. But there were moments in the dark when I lost complete track of time and I was amazed

when the door opened and somebody told me the school day was over because I thought it was too soon. Pre was acting as a mentor at the junior high and we'd see him running usually up and down the halls from one thing to another and as things progressed we shared a track with the high school and as we were getting a little bit older still at the junior high we were allowed in our offseason to go to start training with the high school and the story goes one day I went over with a couple other boys and I said to the coach Harry Johnson who we'd never met before it had been pre-arranged that we were going to come over but I said hi coach Johnson we're the boys from Roosevelt and he said we only have men on this team which was really

the perfect thing to say and won us over completely because our school theater production now for two years running at Roosevelt had been a modernized adaptation of Taming of the Shrew entitled Miz and calling any 14 year old female at my school girl got you an immediate lecture but nobody ever called us men but that was the situation we were working with Harry the South Eugene high school track program in the 70s was the best high school track program and our work was pretty well laid out for us twice a day workouts every day of high school I had a class first period that was called running which was just a way for me to have time to do my morning workout and through the years in high school starting

ninth grade south began setting national high school records in relay events I was able to be part of one of those in my junior year individual national high school records by various friends of mine and an amazing long string of state championships that went for over 12 years we never lacked in self-confidence and it was a time when a kid could dream that maybe he too could be an Olympian but at the end of my ninth grade year came the day that pre died in a car accident just in front of the Alvarado's house a few days later 7,000 of us filled the old wooden East grandstands where just the night before pre died we had been watching his final race in the final mile he had moved away from everyone no one could stay with

him Frank Shorter was in the race and afterwards said he was just beyond me at that point he missed his own American record by less than two seconds and you'll know that it's that race if you see a picture of him wearing a black singlet because it's the only race in his life that he wore a black singlet we filed into these grandstands and the stadium clock was started and set to stop at what some felt would have been for pre a satisfactory world record for three miles as the clock ran first Bowerman and then shorter and finally Kenny Moore who besides being gotten fourth in the Munich Marathon was also world-class sports writer spoke more said he conceived of the sport as service in the way an artist serves

without that he would never given us all the records they were out beyond winning or losing which a runner does for himself they came from those furious minutes near the end of a race when his relentlessness and our excitement blended into a joyous thunder all of us who now say I had no idea how much this man meant to me do so because we didn't realize how much we meant to him he was our glory and we his then he stepped away from the podium then stepped back and said there are two minutes on the clock he could run a half a mile then we all waited in silence 7,000 people for a minute and a half nothing had been indicated of how this would finish other than the clock running out but with 30 seconds to go I like everyone

else looked over at the 200 meters to go mark and as the imaginary runner was coming around the bend a truly amazing display of public ceremony spontaneously unfolded as first from the left and then traveling all down the grandstand the crowd applauded in a rolling wave that finally trickled out at the finish line and was over the clock stopped and the silence swept back to fill the space now the rock outcropping a couple blocks distance about the house I grew up in where Pree's MG overturned has become a devotional site at any time and especially when a major meat is in town the rock is festooned with offerings meat ribbons someone's race numbers from Boston state championship medals shoes t-shirts runners

and athletes from all over the world leave items of significance at this spot to remember this person who inspired so many that summer my family bought a beach cabin on the coast that we vacationed at and instead of renting we'd have a place of our own and my father hired a carpenter and I came to work too for 75 cents an hour the carpenter was John Pound a 40-something hippie artist from California whose work vehicle was a VW van with an American flag draped along the whole ceiling inside think Jimmy Buffett plus 40 pounds and overalls with a pipe clenched in the corner of his mouth and a wry little Santa Claus twinkle in his eye John was a self-taught remodeler experienced

a lot of things willing to try something and he was also an astute observer of the human condition born from his years in therapy very Californian attribute which I thought was interesting and he was extremely accepting and fond of me and was the only person in my life who's ever with any sense of acceptance from me been able to call me Bobby living alone on the coast had its difficulties in loneliness as 15 years old living alone with a bicycle to get around I had no telephone or TV only the radio at night to keep me company and the wide-stretched Oregon beaches are not sort of place to go and meet people it's the kind of place people go to be alone but I enjoyed it well enough and I came

back the following summer and did the same thing high school my friend Jeff another runner and I had started getting into bowhunting I'd always done archery since childhood taught by my mother who had been taught by my grandfather I'd always been inspired by my grandfather who had died when I was 11 a man with a quiet and deeply assured bearing hunter and fisherman who attended his half acre garden at his place on the banks of the rogue river where he pulled steel head out from his walking dock and where he would wash newly pulled carrots for me in the irrigation ditch beside the great barbers and raspberries now on weekend trips Jeff and I would drive high into the dark coast range on early foggy

mornings before dawn and stalk through the woods and camouflage clothing covered in deer musk scent moving as quietly as possible and listening at other times we'd travel over the mountains to camp in the junipers and stalk through the hard frost sagebrush hunting jackrabbits which with a bow it's no wonder we never got one but we did get shots we never managed to take a shot at a deer though I did have one encounter in the deeply twilight woods a silhouette that looked like it had antlers my hand trembling on the string the darkness growing and inside the jackhammer heart pounding my legs quivering sweat immediately beating up almost feeling like I couldn't breathe after this I decided I probably did not want to go

through with the whole killing thing and when I went to college I became a vegetarian which for me was really an extension of the same thoughts about food each year in high school I would ride my bike on one spring weekend out to mount pisca on the edge of town and camp out alone for the night and on these trips I would always try to go back into the woods to find deer I'd try to get as close as possible and feel the deer's presence and become part of its world I felt I had an almost mystical feeling about them and when I could have an encounter like that it always felt special now the summer before my senior year a few blocks away my dad's best friend from college ed frazier an editorial

page columnist for the Eugene registered guard got up after dinner after dinner went into the bathroom took out a pistol and shot himself in the head he didn't leave a note I can only imagine what my father's feelings were it wasn't as though we had the kind of relationship where he would come lean on me but one day a couple weeks after it happened he turned to me with this pained look and simply said why would someone do that and I knew what he was referring to then at some point that fall he had another heart attack he was in the hospital for a while then some rest then back to work in a limited way it was scary but I guess filtering through the denial I believed he was going to get through

this already then on new year's eve day coming back from a snow camping trip Jeff and I spontaneously decided to stop and try and climb a huge cliff we saw we only got so far and then I kicked loose a 300 pound boulder and the boulder and I went careening down the slope together it rolled over my leg twice then was coming from my head I got my hands on it and finally pushed myself clear my right calf was crushed but the bone wasn't broken I was six weeks on crutches each day to the pool to swim and keep fitness then two weeks walking two weeks jogging finally actual running and then while helping with field events I got hit in the leg in the same spot by a discus finally I made it to the district meet but by

that point my father back at home was growing sicker and sicker at the district meet only the top two qualified for state by the top of the final turn I'd forged up to the shoulder of the early leader but then two more came up and for a moment we were four breast and then that was it there was nothing left the three drifted away I was a second behind the line but at this point it didn't really matter I felt at least I was running someone was waving to me beside the track it was my father in his wheelchair he had insisted that my sister bring him to the meet I had no idea he would be there but he waved me over and we hugged and it really made the whole experience much more tolerable
